opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's something I think about a lot. The way I'd frame it is that HippoRAG was never really meant to be in competition with long-context models. If anything, I think of them as complementary pieces of the same memory system.

If you take the hippocampal analogy seriously, the hippocampus isn't where you do your thinking. It's an index. It points you to the right pieces of experience so the neocortex can actually work with them. A long-context model is, in a sense, a much bigger, more capable "working space" for that neocortical reasoning. So if resources aren't a concern, the natural design is: use the knowledge graph and Personalized PageRank to figure out *what* is relevant, especially the multi-hop, associative stuff that dense retrieval misses, and then hand a much larger, richer set of those passages to a long-context model to reason over. Instead of retrieving the top five passages, maybe you retrieve the top fifty, or entire documents, and you let the model do the fine-grained integration.

The reason you still want the index, even with huge context windows, is that context isn't free in terms of quality either. We've seen that models get distracted, they lose things in the middle, and they do worse when a lot of the context is noise. So retrieval becomes less about squeezing into a budget and more about curation, about giving the model a coherent, associatively connected slice of memory rather than a dump of everything.

On consolidation, that's where I think things get really interesting. In the brain, there's this idea that memories get replayed and gradually integrated into the neocortex over time, so you're not just storing raw episodes forever. The analogue for us would be periodically taking clusters of related documents, the ones that keep getting co-retrieved or that are densely connected in the graph, and using a strong long-context model to synthesize them into consolidated summaries, resolve contradictions, update entities, that kind of thing. Then those consolidated nodes become part of the index themselves. So you end up with a kind of hierarchy: raw episodic passages at the bottom, more abstracted, consolidated knowledge above them, and retrieval can operate across both levels.

Without resource constraints, you could run that consolidation pretty aggressively, almost like a sleep phase for the system, and you could also use the long-context model to do much higher-quality open information extraction when building the graph in the first place, looking at whole documents instead of individual passages so you get better entity resolution and cross-passage relations.

The caveat I'd add is that you don't want consolidation to destroy the originals. One of the nice things about non-parametric memory is that it's faithful. You can always go back to the source. So I'd keep the raw episodes and treat consolidated knowledge as an additional layer, not a replacement. That way you get the efficiency and abstraction of consolidation without losing provenance or the ability to correct things when the summary got it wrong.

r001.rationale: Proposes periodically using a strong long-context model to resolve contradictions and update entities during consolidation, which would correct the evolving graph.

r002.rationale: Proposes grouping related or densely connected documents and synthesizing them into consolidated summaries.

r003.rationale: Discusses how long-context models complement HippoRAG, but does not raise or address how far HippoRAG can go without them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because the way we built HippoRAG was really shaped by trying to do things cheaply. The whole point of the offline indexing step, running open information extraction over every passage and building this knowledge graph, is that you pay the cost once and then retrieval is very fast. Personalized PageRank over the graph is basically free at query time. But if you tell me I don't have to worry about cost, I think the picture changes in a couple of ways.

The first thing I'd do is let the long-context model play a much bigger role in the consolidation phase. Right now, when we extract triples, we're doing it passage by passage, and that's a real limitation. The hippocampus analogy we lean on is that the memory system is supposed to integrate information across experiences, not just store each one independently. So if I have a model that can read, say, a hundred related documents at once, I'd want it to do that integration directly. Resolve entity coreference across documents, notice that "the company" in one passage is the same as the named firm in another, merge nodes that should obviously be merged, and maybe even write summary nodes that sit above the raw triples. That's much closer to what consolidation actually means in the neuroscience sense, and it's something we really can't do well with a small model looking at one passage at a time.

The second thing is on the retrieval side. One honest critique of HippoRAG is that it can over-commit to the graph structure. If the extraction missed something, you're stuck. With a long-context model and no budget pressure, I'd use the graph as the first pass, to pull in a candidate neighborhood of documents, and then hand that whole neighborhood to the long-context model and let it do the final reasoning over raw text. So the graph gives you the associative jump, the multi-hop connectivity that dense retrieval struggles with, and the long-context model gives you the fidelity that a compressed triple representation loses.

What I wouldn't do, even with unlimited resources, is just throw everything into context and skip the structure entirely. People have tested this, and long-context models still degrade when the relevant information is scattered across a huge input, especially for multi-hop questions where you need to connect two things that are far apart. The graph is doing real work there. It's not just a cost-saving trick, it's an inductive bias about how memories should be linked. So I see it as complementary. Structure for navigation, long context for understanding, and ideally the long-context model helps build better structure in the first place.

r001.rationale: Proposes using a long-context model during consolidation to resolve cross-document coreference and merge nodes, improving the knowledge graph as it is built.

r002.rationale: Proposes processing groups of related documents together and potentially creating summary nodes above the raw triples, which conveys cluster-based summarization.

r003.rationale: It says passage-by-passage extraction is limited and describes long-context models as complementary, but does not raise the question of how far HippoRAG can go without them.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. If we’re not tightly constrained by compute or latency, I wouldn’t view HippoRAG as a substitute for long context. I’d use it to find the relevant information and make connections across documents, and then give the language model a richer set of those documents to reason over. A larger context window lets us preserve more of the surrounding evidence instead of forcing everything into tiny retrieved passages.

Document consolidation could help at a different stage. When several documents discuss the same entity or event, we could bring that information together, resolve references, and build a more coherent representation for retrieval. But I’d preserve the original sources alongside that representation, because consolidation can lose details or smooth over disagreements that matter to the question.

So the system I’d want would have both: a consolidated representation that helps it navigate the collection, and access to the underlying documents through a long-context model. Retrieval helps decide what deserves attention; long context gives the model room to examine that evidence in depth. Removing resource constraints makes that combination more attractive, but we’d still need to test whether each additional piece of context actually improves the answer.

r001.rationale: The response pairs retrieval with long-context reasoning, but does not propose using long-context models to correct an evolving HippoRAG knowledge graph.

r002.rationale: It proposes combining information about entities or events into a coherent representation, but does not describe cluster-based summarization.

r003.rationale: It says HippoRAG and long-context models are complementary; it does not raise how far HippoRAG can go without long-context models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very complementary. If you don’t have tight resource constraints, you can use a long-context model to read more of the original documents after HippoRAG has identified the relevant parts of the corpus. The retrieval system helps you decide what deserves attention, and the long context gives the model room to interpret that information together.

Document consolidation can help at a different stage. If several documents describe the same entity or event, bringing that information together can make connections more explicit and make retrieval easier. But I would preserve the original documents and the links back to them, because consolidation can lose details or hide disagreements between sources.

So I’d want a system that can move between levels: consolidated information for finding connections, and original passages for checking those connections and answering the question. Even with a large context window, selecting the right evidence is still useful. The goal is to give the model enough context to reason well, while keeping track of where its evidence comes from.

r001.rationale: It proposes using long-context models to interpret retrieved original documents, but does not say they should correct HippoRAG’s evolving knowledge graph.

r002.rationale: It suggests bringing together information about the same entity or event, but does not propose cluster-based summarization.

r003.rationale: It says evidence selection remains useful even with a large context window, but does not ask how far HippoRAG can go without long-context models.
